title: The heart, blood vessels and blood

tips.title: Arteries away, veins in
tips.body: **A**rteries carry blood **a**way from the heart. **Ve**ins carry it back **in** to the heart. The definition is the **direction**, not whether the blood is oxygenated — which is why the **pulmonary artery** carries **deoxygenated** blood and is still an artery.

tips.title: The two pulmonary vessels break the usual rule
tips.body: Almost every artery carries oxygenated blood and almost every vein carries deoxygenated blood. The **pulmonary artery** (heart to lungs) and the **pulmonary vein** (lungs to heart) are the exceptions, and questions are set on exactly these two.

tips.title: Left ventricle thickest, and say how far
tips.body: Left ventricle **thicker than** right ventricle **thicker than** atria. The reason is **distance**: the left pumps to the **whole body**, the right only to the **lungs**, and the atria only to the ventricle next door. Give the comparison and the distance, not just *it is thicker*.

tips.title: Cardiac output rearranges like any product
tips.body: $\text{cardiac output} = \text{stroke volume} \times \text{heart rate}$. Given the output and one of the others, **divide**. The units check it: $\text{cm}^3$ per beat $\times$ beats per minute gives $\text{cm}^3$ per minute.

tips.title: Red cells lost their nucleus for a reason
tips.body: A red blood cell has **no nucleus**, which leaves **more room for haemoglobin**, and a **biconcave** shape, which gives a **large surface area** for oxygen to diffuse across. Both features are answers to the same question: how do you carry the most oxygen possible?

why.matters:
An exchange surface is only useful if something carries the goods away, and that is what this system is. Every part of it is shaped by the job it does and the **pressure** it works at — which is why you can look at a vessel, or a heart chamber, and say what it is for.

The organising idea is the **double** circulation: blood goes through the heart twice on each circuit, once to the lungs and once to the body. Almost every detail here follows from that one arrangement.

examples.title: Why one side of the heart is three times the other
examples.body:
Cut a heart in half and the left ventricle wall is obviously thicker — about **1.2 cm** against **0.4 cm**. It is not a defect and it is not because the left side does more work per beat: both ventricles pump the **same volume**.

The difference is distance. The right ventricle pumps to the lungs, which are next door and whose delicate capillaries would burst at high pressure. The left pumps to everywhere else — up to your head and down to your feet — and needs the pressure to get there. Thicker muscle, higher pressure, longer journey.

examples.title: The cell that threw away its nucleus
examples.body:
A red blood cell is the most specialised cell in the body, and it has given up more than any other to do one job. It has **no nucleus** — the space is used for haemoglobin instead — and it is **biconcave**, a disc dented on both sides, which gives it more surface for its volume.

The price is that it cannot make new proteins or repair itself, so it wears out in about **120 days** and has to be replaced. That is a bargain the body makes deliberately: a cell that carries more oxygen and lives four months beats one that carries less and lives for ever.

examples.title: Why a nurse takes blood from a vein and feels a pulse in an artery
examples.body:
A pulse is the surge of an artery wall as the heart beats, and you can feel it because arteries are **thick, muscular and elastic** — they have to hold blood at the pressure the ventricle produced. Veins are nowhere near that pressure, so there is no pulse to feel.

That same difference decides where a needle goes. A vein is close to the surface, thin-walled and at low pressure, so it can be entered easily and seals again afterwards. It also explains **valves**: with so little pressure left, something has to stop the blood falling back down your legs.

steps.title: What blood is made of
steps.body:
**Blood has four components**, and the spec asks you to relate the structure of each to its function.

**Red blood cells (erythrocytes)** — they **carry oxygen**. Three adaptations:

- they contain **haemoglobin**, which binds oxygen to form **oxyhaemoglobin** in the lungs and releases it in the tissues
- they have **no nucleus**, leaving **more room for haemoglobin**
- they are **biconcave discs** — dented on both sides — giving a **large surface area** for oxygen to diffuse across

**White blood cells** — they **defend against pathogens**, and there are two kinds:

- **phagocytes** **engulf and digest** pathogens
- **lymphocytes** **produce antibodies**

Unlike red blood cells, white blood cells **do have a nucleus**, which is how they are told apart under a microscope.

**Plasma** — the straw-coloured **liquid** that everything else is carried in. It **transports** carbon dioxide, **urea**, **hormones**, **digested food molecules** such as glucose and amino acids, and **heat** around the body, as well as the blood cells themselves.

**Platelets** — **fragments of cells** that cause **blood clotting** at a wound. The clot seals the wound, which **stops blood loss** and **stops pathogens entering**. Both halves of that are worth giving.

**Notice the pattern in the red blood cell.** Every one of its features answers the same question — *how do you carry as much oxygen as possible?* — which makes them easier to recall than three separate facts.

steps.title: The three blood vessels
steps.body:
**Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins carry blood towards the heart.** That is the definition, and it is about **direction**, not about oxygen.

**Arteries** carry blood that has just been pushed out by the ventricles, so it is at **high pressure**. Their structure follows:

- **thick walls** containing **muscle** and **elastic fibres**, to **withstand** the pressure without bursting and to **stretch and recoil** as each surge passes
- a **narrow lumen**, which helps keep the pressure high
- **no valves**, except where they leave the heart — the pressure is enough to keep blood moving forwards

**Veins** carry blood at **low pressure**, because it has already been through the capillaries:

- **thin walls**, since there is little pressure to resist
- a **wide lumen**, which reduces resistance to flow
- **valves**, to **prevent backflow** — essential, because the pressure is too low to guarantee one-way flow on its own

**Capillaries** are where the exchange happens:

- walls **one cell thick**, giving a **short diffusion distance**
- **permeable**, so substances can pass through
- so **narrow** that red blood cells pass in single file, which slows them and brings them close to the wall

**The valve question is worth understanding rather than memorising.** Blood in the veins of your legs has to travel **upwards against gravity** at low pressure. Valves let the squeeze of surrounding muscles push it forwards and stop it falling back — which is why standing still for a long time makes your feet swell.

steps.title: The heart, and the double circulatory system
steps.body:
**The heart has four chambers**: a **right atrium** and **right ventricle**, and a **left atrium** and **left ventricle**. The **atria** are the upper chambers that receive blood; the **ventricles** are the lower chambers that pump it out.

**The four major blood vessels**, and what each does:

- **Vena cava** — brings **deoxygenated** blood from the body into the **right atrium**
- **Pulmonary artery** — carries **deoxygenated** blood from the **right ventricle** to the **lungs**
- **Pulmonary vein** — brings **oxygenated** blood from the **lungs** into the **left atrium**
- **Aorta** — carries **oxygenated** blood from the **left ventricle** to the **body**

**Those two pulmonary vessels are the exception to the usual rule.** An artery is defined by carrying blood **away from the heart**, and the pulmonary artery does — to the lungs — even though its blood is **deoxygenated**. The pulmonary vein carries **oxygenated** blood back. Questions are set on exactly this pair.

**The double circulatory system.** Blood passes through the heart **twice** for each complete circuit of the body:

1. Right side → **lungs** → back to the heart. This is the **pulmonary** circuit.
2. Left side → **body** → back to the heart. This is the **systemic** circuit.

**Why have two?** Because blood leaving the lungs has lost most of its pressure in the delicate lung capillaries. Returning it to the heart lets it be **re-pressurised** before being sent round the body, so it travels **faster** and delivers oxygen more quickly than a single circuit could.

**Valves inside the heart** prevent backflow between atrium and ventricle, and out of the ventricles into the arteries.

steps.title: Why the chamber walls differ in thickness
steps.body:
**The walls of the four chambers are not the same thickness, and the differences are examinable.**

**Atria have thinner walls than ventricles.** An atrium only has to push blood into the **ventricle immediately below it** — a few centimetres. It needs very little force.

**The left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right.** Both hold the **same volume** of blood and pump it at the **same time**, but they send it to very different places:

- the **right ventricle** pumps to the **lungs**, which are **close by**
- the **left ventricle** pumps to the **whole body**, including the head and the feet

So the left ventricle must generate a **much higher pressure**, and a thicker muscular wall contracts more **forcefully** to do it.

**There is a second reason, and it is the better one to give.** If the right ventricle pumped as hard as the left, the **high pressure would damage the delicate capillaries in the lungs** — the very vessels whose thin walls make gas exchange possible. So the right ventricle is not merely *good enough*; it is deliberately **weaker**.

**The trap.** *The left ventricle is thicker because it carries more blood* is wrong. Both ventricles pump the **same volume**; the difference is the **distance** and therefore the **pressure**.

**A good answer names both chambers and the distance**: *the left ventricle wall is thicker than the right because it pumps blood to the whole body rather than just to the lungs, so it must produce a higher pressure.*

steps.title: Cardiac output
steps.body:
**Spec point 8.12** gives one equation:

$$\text{cardiac output} = \text{stroke volume} \times \text{heart rate}$$

- **Stroke volume** is the volume of blood pumped out of the left ventricle in **one beat**, in cm³.
- **Heart rate** is the number of **beats per minute**.
- **Cardiac output** is therefore the volume pumped **per minute**, in cm³/min.

**The units check the working.** Cubic centimetres **per beat**, multiplied by beats **per minute**, gives cubic centimetres **per minute** — the beats cancel. If your units do not cancel like that, the numbers have been put in the wrong places.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**An artery is defined by direction, so the pulmonary artery is not an exception to the definition.** It is only an exception to the **usual pattern** of oxygenated blood. Saying *arteries carry oxygenated blood* is a generalisation with two named counterexamples on the syllabus, and a question naming the pulmonary vessels is testing precisely whether you learned the rule or the definition.

**Thickness is about distance, not volume.** Both ventricles hold the **same volume** and contract **together**. The left wall is thicker because it pumps to the **whole body** and so must generate a far higher **pressure**. The strongest answers add the second reason: the right ventricle is deliberately weaker because **high pressure would damage the thin-walled capillaries in the lungs**, which are thin precisely so that gas exchange can happen. One structure protecting another is a grade 9 observation.

**Every red blood cell feature answers one question.** *How do you carry the most oxygen?* **Haemoglobin** binds it; **no nucleus** leaves room for more haemoglobin; the **biconcave** shape gives a large **surface area** so it loads and unloads quickly. Presented as one idea, it is far harder to forget than three.

**Say what a clot does, twice.** Platelets cause clotting, and the clot both **stops blood loss** and **stops pathogens entering**. The second half is the one usually missed, and it links this topic to immunity.

**Cardiac output questions are really about fitness.** A trained athlete has a **larger stroke volume**, so the **same** cardiac output is achieved at a **lower heart rate** — 80 cm³ at 60 bpm against 70 cm³ at 72 bpm. A low resting pulse is therefore a sign of a **strong** heart, not a weak one, and being able to say why from the equation is what the question is for.

**Let the units check you.** cm³ **per beat** times beats **per minute** gives cm³ **per minute**. If the beats do not cancel, the numbers are in the wrong places — a check that works without knowing the answer.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Red blood cells** carry **oxygen**: they contain **haemoglobin**, have **no nucleus** (more room for haemoglobin) and are **biconcave** (large surface area).
- Haemoglobin binds oxygen to form **oxyhaemoglobin** in the lungs and releases it in the tissues.
- **White blood cells**: **phagocytes engulf and digest** pathogens; **lymphocytes produce antibodies**. They **have a nucleus**.
- **Plasma** is the liquid that transports **carbon dioxide, urea, hormones, digested food and heat**, as well as the cells.
- **Platelets** are **cell fragments** that cause **clotting**, which **stops blood loss** and **stops pathogens entering**.
- **Arteries carry blood away from the heart**; **veins carry it towards** the heart. The definition is **direction**.
- **Arteries**: **thick muscular and elastic walls**, **narrow lumen**, **high pressure**, no valves except at the heart.
- **Veins**: **thin walls**, **wide lumen**, **low pressure**, and **valves to prevent backflow**.
- **Capillaries**: walls **one cell thick** for a **short diffusion distance**, and **permeable** for exchange.
- The heart has four chambers: **right and left atria** (upper, receive) and **right and left ventricles** (lower, pump).
- **Vena cava** → right atrium. **Pulmonary artery** → lungs. **Pulmonary vein** → left atrium. **Aorta** → body.
- The **pulmonary artery** carries **deoxygenated** blood and the **pulmonary vein** carries **oxygenated** blood: the two exceptions.
- The circulation is **double**: blood passes through the heart **twice** per circuit, so it can be **re-pressurised** after the lungs.
- **Atria have thin walls**; the **left ventricle is thickest** because it pumps to the **whole body**.
- The right ventricle is weaker so that **high pressure does not damage the lung capillaries**.
- $\text{cardiac output} = \text{stroke volume} \times \text{heart rate}$, giving **cm³ per minute**.
- A **trained athlete** has a **larger stroke volume**, so the same output needs a **lower heart rate**.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of the heart and explain how blood travels through it in a double circulatory system. Include the four major blood vessels and explain why the ventricle walls differ in thickness.
questions.solution:
The heart has **four chambers**. The two upper chambers, the **right and left atria**, **receive** blood arriving at the heart; the two lower chambers, the **right and left ventricles**, **pump** it out. **Valves** between the atria and ventricles, and at the exits of the ventricles, prevent **backflow**.

Blood arrives from the body through the **vena cava**, which empties **deoxygenated** blood into the **right atrium**. From there it passes into the **right ventricle**, which pumps it out through the **pulmonary artery** to the **lungs**. In the lungs it is oxygenated, and returns through the **pulmonary vein** into the **left atrium**. It passes into the **left ventricle**, which pumps it out through the **aorta** to the rest of the body.

Those two pulmonary vessels are worth noting carefully. The **pulmonary artery** carries **deoxygenated** blood and the **pulmonary vein** carries **oxygenated** blood — the opposite of the usual pattern. They are still an artery and a vein, because a vessel is classified by **direction**: arteries carry blood **away from** the heart and veins carry it **towards** the heart.

This arrangement is a **double circulatory system**: blood passes through the heart **twice** for each complete circuit of the body, once on the **pulmonary** circuit to the lungs and once on the **systemic** circuit to the body. The advantage is one of **pressure**. The capillaries in the lungs are extremely narrow and thin-walled, and blood loses most of its pressure passing through them. Returning it to the heart allows it to be **re-pressurised** before being sent round the body, so it flows **faster** and delivers oxygen more quickly than a single circuit could manage.

The **ventricle walls** differ for the same reason. Both ventricles hold the **same volume** of blood and contract at the **same time**, so the difference is not how much they pump but **how far**. The **left ventricle** pumps blood to the **whole body**, so it must generate a much **higher pressure**, and its thicker muscular wall contracts more forcefully to do so. The **right ventricle** pumps only to the nearby **lungs**. Crucially, it is not merely *strong enough* — it is deliberately **weaker**, because a pressure as high as the left ventricle's would **damage the delicate capillaries in the lungs**, whose thin walls are exactly what makes gas exchange possible.

questions.modelAnswer:
The heart has **four chambers**. The two upper chambers, the **right and left atria**, **receive** blood arriving at the heart; the two lower chambers, the **right and left ventricles**, **pump** it out. **Valves** between the atria and ventricles, and at the exits of the ventricles, prevent **backflow**.

Blood arrives from the body through the **vena cava**, which empties **deoxygenated** blood into the **right atrium**. From there it passes into the **right ventricle**, which pumps it out through the **pulmonary artery** to the **lungs**. In the lungs it is oxygenated, and returns through the **pulmonary vein** into the **left atrium**. It passes into the **left ventricle**, which pumps it out through the **aorta** to the rest of the body.

Those two pulmonary vessels are worth noting carefully. The **pulmonary artery** carries **deoxygenated** blood and the **pulmonary vein** carries **oxygenated** blood — the opposite of the usual pattern. They are still an artery and a vein, because a vessel is classified by **direction**: arteries carry blood **away from** the heart and veins carry it **towards** the heart.

This arrangement is a **double circulatory system**: blood passes through the heart **twice** for each complete circuit of the body, once on the **pulmonary** circuit to the lungs and once on the **systemic** circuit to the body. The advantage is one of **pressure**. The capillaries in the lungs are extremely narrow and thin-walled, and blood loses most of its pressure passing through them. Returning it to the heart allows it to be **re-pressurised** before being sent round the body, so it flows **faster** and delivers oxygen more quickly than a single circuit could manage.

The **ventricle walls** differ for the same reason. Both ventricles hold the **same volume** of blood and contract at the **same time**, so the difference is not how much they pump but **how far**. The **left ventricle** pumps blood to the **whole body**, so it must generate a much **higher pressure**, and its thicker muscular wall contracts more forcefully to do so. The **right ventricle** pumps only to the nearby **lungs**. Crucially, it is not merely *strong enough* — it is deliberately **weaker**, because a pressure as high as the left ventricle's would **damage the delicate capillaries in the lungs**, whose thin walls are exactly what makes gas exchange possible.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of red blood cells, white blood cells, plasma and platelets each suits its function, and how the structure of arteries, veins and capillaries suits theirs.
questions.skill: structure and function in the circulation
questions.solution:
Every feature of a **red blood cell** answers one question: how do you carry as much **oxygen** as possible? It is packed with **haemoglobin**, which binds oxygen in the lungs to form **oxyhaemoglobin** and releases it in the tissues. It has **no nucleus**, which leaves **more room for haemoglobin** and so more oxygen per cell. And it is a **biconcave disc**, dented on both sides, which gives a **large surface area** relative to its volume so that oxygen diffuses in and out quickly.

**White blood cells** defend the body, and there are two kinds with different methods. **Phagocytes** **engulf and digest** pathogens. **Lymphocytes** **produce antibodies** against them. Unlike red blood cells they **retain a nucleus**, which is how the two are distinguished under a microscope.

**Platelets** are **fragments of cells** that cause **blood clotting** at a wound. A clot does two jobs, and both are worth stating: it **stops further blood loss**, and it **seals the wound against pathogens** that would otherwise enter.

**Plasma** is the straw-coloured **liquid** in which everything else travels. It transports **carbon dioxide** from respiring tissues, **urea** from the liver to the kidneys, **hormones**, **digested food molecules** such as glucose and amino acids, and **heat** around the body.

The vessels are shaped by **pressure**. **Arteries** carry blood just pushed out by the ventricles, so it is at **high pressure**: they have **thick walls** with **muscle and elastic fibres** to withstand it and to **stretch and recoil** with each surge, and a **narrow lumen** that helps keep the pressure up. **Veins** carry blood that has already passed through capillaries, so the pressure is **low**: they have **thin walls**, a **wide lumen** to reduce resistance, and **valves** to **prevent backflow**, which matters most in the legs where blood must travel upwards against gravity. **Capillaries** are where exchange happens, so their walls are just **one cell thick**, giving the shortest possible **diffusion distance**, and they are **permeable** and so narrow that red blood cells pass in single file, close to the wall.

examTechnique.body:
This topic rewards **precision about definitions**. An artery is defined by **direction**, not by oxygen, and the two pulmonary vessels exist on the syllabus mainly to test that. Similarly, ventricle wall thickness is about **distance and pressure**, never about volume.

The calculation is short, and the **units** do the checking: cm³ per beat times beats per minute gives cm³ per minute. Use that to confirm a rearrangement rather than trusting the algebra.
examinerErrors: Defining an artery as carrying **oxygenated** blood, which the **pulmonary artery** contradicts.
Saying the left ventricle is thicker because it **holds more blood** — both ventricles hold the **same volume**.
Giving only *it pumps further* without naming **both** chambers and the **pressure** that follows.
Saying a clot only **stops bleeding**, and omitting that it also **stops pathogens entering**.
Confusing **phagocytes**, which engulf and digest, with **lymphocytes**, which make antibodies.
Placing **valves** in arteries generally, rather than in **veins** and at the exits of the heart.
Dividing when the question needs a product, or multiplying when it needs a division, in the cardiac output equation.
Treating a **low resting heart rate** as a sign of a weak heart rather than a **large stroke volume**.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer gives the **definition** rather than the pattern: arteries carry blood **away from the heart**, so the **pulmonary artery** is not an anomaly at all. It explains ventricle thickness by **distance and pressure** and then adds the protective reason — a stronger right ventricle would **damage the lung capillaries**, which are thin precisely so gas exchange can happen. It presents the red blood cell as **one idea in three forms**, and it reads a cardiac output question as a question about **fitness**, showing from the equation why a **larger stroke volume** lets a trained heart beat more slowly. Throughout, it lets the **units** confirm the arithmetic.
